tool.name: Apache Cassandra
tool.tagline: Masterless wide-column database for huge write volumes and always-on availability
tool.description: Apache Cassandra is a distributed, masterless wide-column database designed to stay available across machines and data centers with no single point of failure. You model tables around your queries in CQL, an SQL-like language, and it scales linearly by adding nodes. It is used for time-series, messaging, IoT and other high-write workloads at very large scale.

glossary.def: One server running Cassandra. Many nodes together form a cluster, and all of them are equal.
Having no main server in charge: every node can accept reads and writes, so losing any one machine doesn't stop the database.
A group of Cassandra nodes in one location, such as one building or one cloud region. A cluster can span several, so it survives losing a whole site.
In Cassandra: all the rows that share one partition key value. They are stored together on the same nodes and are read most efficiently as a unit.
The first part of a Cassandra primary key. Its value decides which partition a row belongs to, and so which nodes store it.
In Cassandra: the number a partition key is hashed to. Each node is responsible for a range of tokens, so the token decides where a partition is stored.
All possible Cassandra tokens arranged in a circle and split into ranges that nodes own; a partition's copies are found by walking around it.
How many copies of each partition Cassandra keeps, set per keyspace and per data center; 3 is typical.
The Cassandra node that receives a client's request. It forwards the request to the replicas, gathers their answers and replies.
How many replicas must answer before Cassandra reports a read or write as done, chosen per request: ONE, QUORUM, ALL and so on.
Cassandra Query Language: Cassandra's SQL-like language for creating tables and for reading and writing data.
Cassandra's interactive client: you type CQL statements and see the results, much like psql for PostgreSQL.
The top-level container for Cassandra tables, like a database in SQL. It also sets how many copies of the data to keep, and where.
A file on each Cassandra node that every write is appended to first, so recent writes can be recovered after a crash.
A Cassandra maintenance job that compares the copies of the data on different nodes and copies over whatever some of them are missing.
Cassandra's admin command, run on a node: nodetool status, nodetool repair, nodetool flush and so on.
A primary-key column after the partition key. Clustering columns sort the rows inside a partition, on disk, and let you read ranges of them.
A Cassandra column marked STATIC: stored once per partition and shared by all the rows in it.
A CQL id type: a UUID that also records when it was made, so ids are unique and sort by time.
A CQL type you define that groups named parts, like CREATE TYPE address (street text, city text).
A CQL wrapper, frozen<...>, that stores a collection or user-defined type as one value that can only be replaced whole.
A CQL clause that lets a query scan through and throw away data to find matches. It silences an error but can be very slow.
In Cassandra: one column's value in one row. Each cell has its own write timestamp and, optionally, its own expiry time.
The time, in microseconds, attached to every Cassandra cell when it is written; when copies disagree, the newest timestamp wins.
Cassandra's rule for copies of a value that disagree: the one with the newest write timestamp is kept.
Deliberately storing the same data in several tables, each shaped for one query, instead of storing it once and joining tables at read time.
TimeWindowCompactionStrategy: a Cassandra compaction setting that groups data into files by time window, so files whose data has all expired can simply be deleted.
When a replica is down, the coordinator keeps the writes it missed (hints) and replays them when it comes back, for up to 3 hours by default.
Fixing an out-of-date copy during a read: when the replicas a read asked disagree, Cassandra writes the newest value back to the stale ones.
A Cassandra batch that is first saved to a batch log on other nodes, so all its writes eventually apply even if the coordinator fails part way.
A driver setting that computes a request's token and sends it straight to a replica that owns it, saving a hop through another node.
Fetching a long query result one page of rows at a time, picking up where the previous page stopped.
Storage-Attached Indexing: Cassandra 5.0's indexes on non-key columns, built right next to each node's data.
A Cassandra write with a condition (IF NOT EXISTS, IF col = value) that the replicas agree on using Paxos, so only one of several competing writes wins.
A voting procedure that lets several machines agree on exactly one outcome, even if some of them are slow or fail.
The consistency level for the Paxos voting step of a lightweight transaction: SERIAL (all data centers) or LOCAL_SERIAL (the local one only).
Adding a part such as the day, or a small hash number, to a partition key, so that no partition grows without limit or gets all the traffic.
A partition that gets a large share of all traffic, overloading the few nodes that store it while the rest sit idle.
In Cassandra: configurable limits, for example on partition or batch size, that warn or refuse when something risky is attempted.
In Cassandra, streaming means copying large chunks of data directly between nodes, for example when a node joins, leaves or is repaired.
In Cassandra: writing a full memtable out to disk as a new SSTable.
The Cassandra table setting (10 days by default) for how long tombstones are kept; repair must reach every replica within this time.
Deleted data that reappears because a replica missed the delete and the tombstone was removed before repair could tell it.
A tree of hashes that summarises data range by range; comparing two such trees quickly shows which ranges differ, so only those need copying.
Virtual node: one of the many small token ranges each Cassandra node owns (16 by default), which spreads data and rebalancing work evenly.
How Cassandra nodes share news: every second each node swaps state (up or down, load, tokens) with a few others, so it spreads to all.
The Cassandra component that tells nodes which data center and rack every node is in, so copies can be placed on different racks.
A cabinet of servers sharing power and network; Cassandra puts copies on different racks so one rack failing loses no data.
The Cassandra component that hashes partition keys to tokens; the standard one is Murmur3Partitioner.
Cassandra's way of judging whether a node is down: it turns how late the node's gossip messages are into a level of suspicion.

concepts.name: What Cassandra is: a masterless ring
concepts.summary: Cassandra spreads data over many equal machines and keeps several copies of every piece, so it keeps working when machines fail.
concepts.why: Every modeling and consistency rule in Cassandra follows from how it spreads data over many machines with nobody in charge.
concepts.body:
A database like PostgreSQL usually runs on one main server: when it fails, the database is down. **Cassandra** takes another route: it spreads your data over many ordinary servers that work together as one database. Each server is a **node**; the group is a **cluster**. A system whose parts run on several computers like this is called **distributed**.

All nodes are equal. No main server is in charge (Cassandra is **masterless**), so your application can send reads and writes to any node, and no single machine failing stops the database. A cluster can also stretch over several **data centers**: separate sites, often in different cities, so even losing a whole site isn't fatal.

Rows are grouped into **partitions**. All rows that share a value of the **partition key**, say every reading from one sensor, form one partition and are always stored together.

To decide which node stores a partition, Cassandra runs the partition key through a **hash** function, which turns any value into a random-looking number, always the same for the same value. That number is the partition's **token**. Each node is responsible for a range of tokens, so the token tells Cassandra exactly where the partition lives.

Each partition is copied to several nodes, its replicas. The number of copies is the **replication factor**, usually 3, so the data survives a node failing. Adding nodes splits the tokens into smaller shares, so capacity grows roughly in step with the number of nodes.

Each read or write, a **request**, can go to any node. That node becomes the **coordinator** for the request: it forwards it to the replicas and collects their answers.

You also choose, per request, how many replicas must answer: the **consistency level**. Fewer is faster and survives more failures; more makes sure you see the latest data.

What follows from this design:

- reads are fast when they touch one partition; there are no joins and no free-form queries across all the data,
- writes are very cheap (Cassandra just appends them), so you copy the same data into one table per query,
- staying available is favoured over always returning the latest value, though you can tune that.

It fits huge, write-heavy data with questions known in advance: sensor readings, event records, chat messages.
takeaways: All nodes are equal; any node can coordinate a request
Rows live in partitions, placed by hashing the partition key to a token
Each partition is copied to several nodes (the replication factor, typically 3)
Fast single-partition access, no joins: one table per query
pitfalls: Choosing Cassandra for free-form reporting queries, or for relational data that needs many joins.

quiz.q: What decides which nodes store a given row?
options: The order in which rows were inserted
The hash (token) of the row's partition key and the replication settings
The main node of the cluster
quiz.explain: The partition key is hashed to a token; the nodes' token ranges and the replication settings pick the replicas.

concepts.name: cqlsh and keyspaces
concepts.summary: Connect with cqlsh and create keyspaces, which set how many copies of the data to keep in each data center.
concepts.why: Keyspaces set replication for everything inside them, and getting it wrong is painful to fix later.
concepts.body:
**CQL** (Cassandra Query Language) is Cassandra's version of SQL: it looks much like the SQL you know, but follows Cassandra's rules. **cqlsh** is its interactive client, like psql for PostgreSQL: you type CQL and see the results. Run `cqlsh host 9042`; 9042 is the **port**, the numbered door on the server where Cassandra listens for clients.

Handy cqlsh commands: `DESCRIBE KEYSPACES` and `DESCRIBE TABLE t` (show definitions), `USE ks;` (pick a keyspace), `CONSISTENCY QUORUM;` (set the consistency level), `TRACING ON;` (show what each query did inside the cluster) and `EXPAND ON;` (print each row vertically).

A **keyspace** is the top-level grouping of tables, like a database or schema in SQL. It also holds the replication settings for every table inside it: how many copies of each partition to keep, and where.

- `NetworkTopologyStrategy` sets a replication factor per data center, e.g. `{'class': 'NetworkTopologyStrategy', 'dc1': 3, 'dc2': 3}`. Use it for anything real, even with one data center, so adding a second later is easy.
- `SimpleStrategy` takes one `replication_factor`, and is only for trying things out on your own machine.

A replication factor of 3 per data center is the norm. Reading and writing with `QUORUM`, a majority (2 of the 3 copies must answer), you can lose one copy and still get correct answers.

`durable_writes` (default true) makes every write go first to the **commit log**, a file on disk that lets a node recover its recent writes after a crash. Leave it on.

You can change replication later with `ALTER KEYSPACE`, but existing data isn't copied to its new places automatically. Afterwards you run **repair**, a maintenance job that compares the copies and fills in what's missing (or `nodetool rebuild` for a new data center). **nodetool** is Cassandra's admin command, run on a node; data center names in the keyspace must match the ones `nodetool status` shows.
takeaways: cqlsh speaks CQL on port 9042
A keyspace sets replication for all its tables
Use NetworkTopologyStrategy with 3 copies per data center
After changing replication, repair or rebuild to move data
pitfalls: Using SimpleStrategy for the real, live database and struggling when a second data center is added.

quiz.q: Where is the replication factor configured in Cassandra?
quiz.explain: Replication strategy and factor are properties of the keyspace.

concepts.name: Tables, partition keys and clustering columns
concepts.summary: Define a primary key as a partition key that spreads data over nodes, plus clustering columns that sort rows inside a partition.
concepts.why: The primary key is the most important design decision in Cassandra: it fixes which queries are possible and how data spreads.
concepts.body:
CQL tables look like SQL tables, but the **primary key** has two parts with very different jobs:

- the **partition key** (the first part) decides which partition, and therefore which nodes, a row lives on. Rows with the same partition key are stored together,
- the **clustering columns** (the rest) sort the rows **inside** the partition, on disk.

`PRIMARY KEY (user_id)` makes one single-row partition per user. `PRIMARY KEY ((sensor_id, day), ts)` has a composite partition key (the inner parentheses), so each sensor-and-day pair is one partition, and the rows inside it are sorted by `ts`. `PRIMARY KEY (channel_id, sent_at, msg_id)` stores a channel's messages in time order, with `msg_id` breaking ties.

The full primary key identifies exactly one row. Inserting another row with the same key overwrites it; there is no duplicate-key error.

A good partition key spreads data evenly: high cardinality, and no single value that a huge share of rows would have (like one hugely popular account). It also keeps partitions from growing without limit, and it matches your queries, because to read you'll almost always need to supply the whole partition key.

Columns marked `STATIC` are stored once per partition and shared by all its rows, which suits details that belong to the whole partition, such as a channel's name. Table options like `default_time_to_live`, `compaction` and `CLUSTERING ORDER BY` go in the `WITH` clause.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE shop.messages (
  channel_id   uuid,
  sent_at      timestamp,
  msg_id       timeuuid,
  channel_name text STATIC,     -- one value per partition
  author       text,
  body         text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((channel_id), sent_at, msg_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (sent_at DESC, msg_id DESC);

CREATE TABLE shop.readings (
  sensor_id text,
  day       date,
  ts        timestamp,
  value     double,
  PRIMARY KEY ((sensor_id, day), ts)   -- composite partition key
);
takeaways: PRIMARY KEY ((partition key), clustering columns...)
Partition key = placement; clustering columns = sort order inside a partition
Same primary key means the same row: writes overwrite
STATIC columns are stored once per partition
pitfalls: Using a low-cardinality partition key like country, creating a few giant partitions that get most of the traffic.

quiz.q: In PRIMARY KEY ((sensor_id, day), ts), what is the partition key?
quiz.explain: The inner parentheses make sensor_id and day together the composite partition key; ts is a clustering column.

concepts.name: Data types, collections and UDTs
concepts.summary: Use CQL types like uuid, timeuuid, timestamp and decimal, collections (list, set, map), user-defined types and vectors.
concepts.why: Choosing the right types, especially for ids, times and collections, avoids subtle mistakes and slow queries.
concepts.body:
CQL has the usual single-value types: `text`, `int`, `bigint` (big integers), `smallint`, `double` (floating-point), `decimal` (exact, for money), `boolean`, `blob` (raw bytes), `inet` (a network address), `date`, `time`, `timestamp` (to the millisecond) and `duration`.

Ids deserve special attention:

- `uuid` for random ids. A **UUID** is a long random-looking id, like `5b6962dd-3f90-4c93-8f61-eabfa4a803e2`, practically never generated twice; `uuid()` makes one.
- `timeuuid` for ids that also record when they were made (`now()` makes one; `toTimestamp(id)` reads the time back). Ideal as a clustering column for events, because two events in the same millisecond still get different ids, which sort by time.

**Collections** store a few values in one column: `list<text>` (ordered, may repeat), `set<text>` (no repeats) and `map<text, int>` (keys with values). You can change parts in place (`tags = tags + {'sale'}`). Keep them small, because Cassandra always reads a collection whole. Adding to a list isn't safe to repeat (retrying adds the item twice), and some list changes make Cassandra read before it writes, so sets and maps are usually better.

A **user-defined type** (UDT) groups named parts, like a mini row: `CREATE TYPE address (street text, city text)`. Wrap UDTs inside collections, and collections inside collections, in `frozen<...>`: Cassandra then stores the value as one piece that can only be replaced whole, not edited part by part.

`counter` columns can only go up or down, and a table with counters may contain nothing but counters (plus its key).

Cassandra 5.0 adds `vector<float, n>`: a **vector**, a fixed-length list of n numbers. Some tools turn text into such lists, called **embeddings**, where similar meanings give similar numbers, and Cassandra can search for the closest ones (a later lesson).
takeaways: timeuuid gives unique, time-ordered ids; uuid gives random ones
Collections are for small bounded data and are read whole
frozen stores a UDT or collection as one replaceable value
counter tables hold only counters; vector<float, n> is new in 5.0
pitfalls: Using timestamp alone as a clustering column for events: two events in the same millisecond overwrite each other.

quiz.q: Two chat messages arrive in the same millisecond in one channel. Which clustering column keeps both?
quiz.explain: A timeuuid is unique even within the same millisecond and still sorts by time.

concepts.name: INSERT and SELECT with key restrictions
concepts.summary: Write rows with INSERT and read them with SELECT, respecting the rules on which key columns a WHERE clause may filter.
concepts.why: CQL looks like SQL but rejects most queries that don't follow the primary key, so you need its rules to write any reads.
concepts.body:
`INSERT INTO t (cols) VALUES (...)` writes a row; you must give every primary key column. `SELECT` looks familiar too, but the `WHERE` clause is restricted so that every query is efficient:

- you must restrict the **full partition key** with `=` (or `IN`), so the query goes to one known partition,
- clustering columns can be restricted **in order**: equality on earlier ones, and a range (`<`, `>=`...) only on the last one you restrict,
- filtering on regular columns isn't allowed without an index.

Within a partition, rows come back in clustering order, and you can `ORDER BY` a clustering column only in the table's order or its exact reverse. `LIMIT` caps rows and `PER PARTITION LIMIT` caps rows per partition.

If a query breaks these rules, Cassandra refuses with an error suggesting `ALLOW FILTERING`. Adding it makes Cassandra scan and discard data, potentially across the whole cluster; it's acceptable only when the scan is already confined to one small partition. The real fix is a table designed for the query, or an index.

There are no joins, no subqueries (queries nested inside other queries) and no `GROUP BY` on arbitrary columns (`GROUP BY` works only on primary key columns), and aggregates like `COUNT(*)` should be used within a partition. `SELECT JSON` and `INSERT JSON` convert rows to and from JSON, a common text format for data.
concepts.code:
INSERT INTO shop.readings (sensor_id, day, ts, value)
VALUES ('s-17', '2026-10-17', '2026-10-17 09:00:00+0000', 21.5);

-- OK: full partition key + range on the clustering column
SELECT ts, value FROM shop.readings
WHERE sensor_id = 's-17' AND day = '2026-10-17'
  AND ts >= '2026-10-17 08:00:00+0000' AND ts < '2026-10-17 10:00:00+0000';
--  ts                              | value
-- ---------------------------------+-------
--  2026-10-17 09:00:00.000000+0000 |  21.5

-- Rejected: partition key incomplete
SELECT * FROM shop.readings WHERE sensor_id = 's-17';
-- InvalidRequest: ... might involve data filtering ... use ALLOW FILTERING
-- (the full partition key must be restricted)

-- Rejected: filtering on a regular column
SELECT * FROM shop.readings WHERE value > 30;
takeaways: Restrict the full partition key in every normal query
Clustering columns: equality in order, then a range on the last
ORDER BY only in clustering order or its reverse
ALLOW FILTERING means a scan: almost always the wrong fix
pitfalls: Adding ALLOW FILTERING to silence the error, then watching the query run out of time on the live database.

quiz.q: Table key PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), year, month, day). Which WHERE clause is valid without ALLOW FILTERING?
quiz.explain: It restricts the partition key, then clustering columns in order with a range only on the last restricted one.

concepts.name: Upserts, updates and deletes
concepts.summary: Learn that INSERT and UPDATE both insert-or-overwrite, that deletes write tombstones, and how the newest write wins conflicts.
concepts.why: Cassandra's writes behave differently from SQL's, and assuming SQL behaviour leads to silent data surprises.
concepts.body:
In SQL, `INSERT` fails if the row already exists and `UPDATE` does nothing if it doesn't. In Cassandra both are **upserts**: insert the row if it's missing, overwrite it if it's there. `INSERT` on an existing primary key overwrites the given columns; `UPDATE ... WHERE key = ...` on a missing row creates it. Neither looks before writing, which is why writes are so fast, and neither tells you whether the row existed. (When you need that, `IF NOT EXISTS` checks first, at a price; see the lightweight transactions lesson.)

One column's value in one row is a **cell**. Every cell carries a **write timestamp** in microseconds (millionths of a second), set by the coordinator or by your application. When replicas hold different values for the same cell, the newest timestamp wins: **last write wins**. So if two machines' clocks disagree, an older write can beat a newer one; keep all clocks in sync (NTP is the standard tool for that).

A `DELETE` doesn't erase data straight away. It writes a **tombstone**: a marker with its own timestamp saying "deleted", which hides any older values. You can delete a whole partition, a range of rows by clustering column, a single row, or single columns.

The old values and the tombstones are removed later by **compaction**, a cleanup that runs in the background, merging a table's files on disk and throws away what was overwritten or deleted. Tombstones are kept for at least `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days by default) first, so every replica hears about the delete.

Writing `null` into a column also creates a tombstone. Applications talk to Cassandra through a **driver**, a ready-made add-on for the language the application is written in. With a driver you usually run a **prepared statement**: a query written once with `?` placeholders and then run with different values. If your code fills every unused placeholder with `null`, it can create millions of tombstones; leave those values **unset** instead.

`UPDATE` changes only non-key columns. To change a primary key value, delete the old row and insert a new one.
concepts.code:
INSERT INTO shop.users (user_id, email) VALUES (5b6962dd-3f90-4c93-8f61-eabfa4a803e2, 'a@x.io');
INSERT INTO shop.users (user_id, email) VALUES (5b6962dd-3f90-4c93-8f61-eabfa4a803e2, 'b@x.io');
-- no error: the second insert overwrote email

UPDATE shop.users SET email = 'c@x.io'
WHERE user_id = 0d1d8cd6-31ab-4a4b-a6d3-6c0e2b1b9a10;   -- row didn't exist: now it does

SELECT email, WRITETIME(email) FROM shop.users
WHERE user_id = 5b6962dd-3f90-4c93-8f61-eabfa4a803e2;
--  email  | writetime(email)
--  b@x.io | 1760691600123456

DELETE prefs FROM shop.users WHERE user_id = 5b6962dd-3f90-4c93-8f61-eabfa4a803e2; -- column
DELETE FROM shop.readings WHERE sensor_id = 's-17' AND day = '2026-10-17'
  AND ts < '2026-10-17 06:00:00+0000';                                           -- row range
takeaways: INSERT and UPDATE are both upserts and don't read first
Conflicts resolve by highest write timestamp (last write wins)
Deletes and null writes create tombstones, purged after gc_grace_seconds
Leave unused values unset rather than sending null
pitfalls: Expecting INSERT to fail on a duplicate key like in SQL.

quiz.q: You INSERT a row whose primary key already exists. What happens?
quiz.explain: Writes are upserts: same primary key means the same row.

concepts.name: Clustering order and range queries
concepts.summary: Use clustering columns and CLUSTERING ORDER BY to answer latest-first and time-range queries straight from the order on disk.
concepts.why: Feeds and time-ordered queries are fast only when the table's order on disk matches what the query asks for.
concepts.body:
Rows inside a partition are stored sorted by the clustering columns, so a query that reads a continuous slice in that order reads one stretch of disk, front to back. Design the clustering order around your most common query:

- "latest 20 messages" wants `CLUSTERING ORDER BY (sent_at DESC)`, so the newest rows come first and `LIMIT 20` can stop early,
- "readings between 08:00 and 10:00" is a range on the clustering column,
- with several clustering columns, `(year, month, day)`, you can fix the first ones with equality and use a range on the next.

Reading in the reverse of the declared order works (`ORDER BY sent_at ASC` on a DESC table), but reading forward is more efficient, so declare the order your most frequent query uses.

**Paging** means fetching a long result one page at a time. Drivers (the add-ons applications use to talk to Cassandra) page automatically, remembering where they stopped. You can also page by hand with a range on the clustering column: `WHERE channel_id = ? AND sent_at < :last_seen LIMIT 20`.

You can compare several clustering columns as one group, in clustering order: `(sent_at, msg_id) < ('2026-10-17 09:00', ...)`. That's how you continue exactly after the last row you saw when several rows share a timestamp.

The clustering order is fixed when the table is created; changing it means creating a new table and copying the data.
concepts.code:
-- table messages: PRIMARY KEY ((channel_id), sent_at, msg_id)
--                 WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (sent_at DESC, msg_id DESC)

-- newest 20 messages: one sequential read, stops after 20 rows
SELECT sent_at, author, body FROM shop.messages
WHERE channel_id = 6ab09bec-e68e-48d9-a5f8-97e6fb4c9b47
LIMIT 20;

-- next page: continue strictly after the last (sent_at, msg_id) seen
SELECT sent_at, msg_id, body FROM shop.messages
WHERE channel_id = 6ab09bec-e68e-48d9-a5f8-97e6fb4c9b47
  AND (sent_at, msg_id) < ('2026-10-17 09:00:00+0000', 50554d6e-29bb-11ef-9f3c-0242ac120002)
LIMIT 20;

-- reverse order is allowed, but less efficient
SELECT body FROM shop.messages
WHERE channel_id = 6ab09bec-e68e-48d9-a5f8-97e6fb4c9b47
ORDER BY sent_at ASC, msg_id ASC LIMIT 5;
takeaways: Rows are stored sorted by clustering columns within a partition
Declare CLUSTERING ORDER BY to match the most frequent query (often DESC)
Ranges apply to the next clustering column after equality on earlier ones
Comparing (col1, col2) as a group continues paging exactly after the last row
pitfalls: Declaring ascending order for a latest-first feed and paying for reverse reads on every request.

quiz.q: A table has CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC). Which ORDER BY clauses are allowed?
quiz.explain: You may read in the declared order or its exact reverse.

concepts.name: Query-first modeling and denormalization
concepts.summary: Design one table per query, duplicating data across tables, instead of normalizing and joining.
concepts.why: Without joins, the schema must be shaped by the application's queries, which is the core skill of Cassandra.
concepts.body:
Relational design starts from the entities, normalizes them, and lets the database join tables at query time. Cassandra has no joins and little filtering, so you work the other way round: **list the queries first**, then design one table for each, so that the query reads a single partition.

The steps:

- write down every way the application reads data: "messages in a channel, newest first", "channels a user belongs to", "user by email",
- for each, choose a partition key from what the query already knows (`channel_id`, `user_id`, `email`) and clustering columns for the order it wants,
- put every column the query needs into that table.

The result is **denormalized**: the same data is stored in several tables, such as `users_by_id` and `users_by_email`. Writes are cheap, so writing to several tables is fine; the application keeps them in step, often with a logged batch (a group of writes that all eventually apply; see the batches lesson).

Naming tables `<entity>_by_<key>` makes the pattern obvious. Ask of every table: does each query hit exactly one partition, are partitions limited in size, and is data spread evenly?

A many-to-many relationship becomes two tables, one per direction (`members_by_channel`, `channels_by_member`). Totals you need often are kept up to date as you write (counters or summary tables) rather than computed at read time.

Materialized views (tables Cassandra would keep in step with another table for you) exist, but they're marked experimental and switched off by default in recent versions; maintain denormalized tables yourself.
takeaways: List queries first, then design one table per query
Each query should read exactly one partition
Duplicate data across tables; writes are cheap
Name tables <entity>_by_<key>
pitfalls: Porting a normalized relational schema and then needing joins or ALLOW FILTERING for every screen.

quiz.q: The app needs 'orders by user' and 'orders by status for the admin page'. What is the Cassandra approach?
options: One orders table with a secondary index on everything
Store orders in a single partition
A join between users and orders
Two tables, orders_by_user and orders_by_status, written together
quiz.explain: Each access pattern gets its own table keyed for that query.

concepts.name: TTL and write timestamps
concepts.summary: Expire data automatically with USING TTL or a table default, and inspect each cell's write timestamp and remaining time to live.
concepts.why: Login sessions, temporary copies of data and keep-for-30-days rules are all handled by TTL, but expiring data has tombstone costs to plan for.
concepts.body:
Any write can carry a **time to live** (TTL) in seconds: `INSERT ... USING TTL 86400` or `UPDATE t USING TTL 3600 SET ...`. When it runs out, the cell expires and stops being returned. A table can set `default_time_to_live` so every write expires unless it gives its own TTL.

TTL applies per **cell**, not per row: updating one column with a new TTL leaves the others with their old one. `TTL(col)` shows a cell's remaining seconds and `WRITETIME(col)` its write timestamp in microseconds. A TTL of 0 means it never expires.

`USING TIMESTAMP` lets you set the write timestamp yourself. That's useful when you replay the same writes twice and want the same result, or when you load old data in bulk and it must not overwrite newer data. Normally you let the coordinator set it.

Expired cells turn into tombstones, which compaction removes after `gc_grace_seconds`. On disk, a table's data lives in **SSTables**: files that are never changed once written, which compaction merges.

For **time series** (measurements recorded over time) where everything in a table has the same TTL and arrives in time order, use **TimeWindowCompactionStrategy** (TWCS), or UnifiedCompactionStrategy set up the same way. It groups data into SSTables by time window, so a whole file can simply be deleted once everything in it has expired. That's far cheaper than compacting away tombstones one by one.

Avoid mixing data with and without a TTL, or very different TTLs, in one time-series table, because it stops whole files from expiring together.
takeaways: USING TTL per write or default_time_to_live per table
TTL is per cell: updating one column doesn't refresh the others
TTL() and WRITETIME() inspect cells
Expired data becomes tombstones; TWCS deletes whole expired SSTables
pitfalls: Refreshing the TTL on one column and expecting the whole row to live longer.

quiz.q: A row was inserted with TTL 3600 on all columns. Ten minutes later you UPDATE only column b with TTL 3600. When does column a expire?
options: One hour after the original insert
quiz.explain: TTL is tracked per cell, so column a keeps its original expiry.

concepts.name: Tunable consistency
concepts.summary: Choose consistency levels like ONE, QUORUM and LOCAL_QUORUM per request, and reason with the rule R + W > RF.
concepts.why: Consistency level decides whether reads see the latest writes and whether requests succeed when nodes are down.
concepts.body:
Each read and write has a consistency level: how many replicas must confirm before the coordinator answers.

- `ONE`, `TWO`, `THREE`: that many replicas,
- `QUORUM`: a majority of all replicas, across all data centers (2 of 3 with a replication factor of 3),
- `LOCAL_QUORUM`: a majority in the coordinator's own data center, the usual choice for clusters in several data centers,
- `EACH_QUORUM` (writes): a majority in every data center; `ALL`: every replica,
- `LOCAL_ONE`: one replica in the local data center; `ANY` (writes only) is satisfied even by a hint (see below).

Writes are always sent to all replicas; the consistency level only decides how many confirmations to wait for. Reads ask enough replicas to meet the level and return the value with the newest timestamp.

The rule of thumb: with R replicas answering reads, W confirming writes and RF copies in total, if **R + W > RF**, every read reaches at least one replica that has the latest write, so reads always see it (ignoring clock differences). With RF 3, `QUORUM` + `QUORUM` (2 + 2 > 3) always reads the latest write and still works with one replica down. `ONE` + `ONE` is fastest and most available, but may return an out-of-date value.

Replicas that missed writes catch up three ways. **Hinted handoff**: the coordinator keeps the writes a down replica missed, as hints, for up to 3 hours by default, and replays them when it's back. **Read repair**: when replicas answering a read disagree, the newest value is written back to the stale ones. And regular repair compares everything.

A write that failed at its consistency level isn't necessarily undone: some replicas may already have it. So make writes **idempotent** (safe to repeat, giving the same result) so that a **retry**, trying the write again, can't do harm.
takeaways: The consistency level = how many replicas must confirm, chosen per request
R + W > RF means reads always see the latest write
LOCAL_QUORUM is the usual default with several data centers
Hints, read repair and repair bring replicas back in sync
pitfalls: Using ALL for safety: one unavailable replica makes requests fail.

quiz.q: With RF 3, which combination guarantees reads see the latest successful write?
quiz.explain: 2 + 2 > 3, so the read and write replica sets always overlap.

quiz.q: With RF 3 and one replica down, can QUORUM reads and writes still succeed?
quiz.explain: A quorum of 3 is 2, so one replica can be down.

concepts.name: Batches: what they are and are not
concepts.summary: Use logged batches to keep denormalized tables in sync, and avoid batches as a bulk-loading tool.
concepts.why: Batches are the most misused CQL feature: right for multi-table consistency, wrong for performance.
concepts.body:
`BEGIN BATCH ... APPLY BATCH;` groups several writes. Its purpose is **atomicity** (all or nothing), not speed.

A **logged batch** (the default) is first saved to a batch log on other nodes. If the coordinator fails part way, the batch log is replayed, so eventually **all or none** of the statements apply. This is how you keep denormalized tables (`users_by_id` and `users_by_email`) in step. There is no isolation across partitions: a reader may briefly see one table updated and not the other. And there is no rollback.

A batch whose statements all target the **same partition** is applied on each replica as one single change, atomic and isolated, with no batch log needed. That's efficient and a good use of batches.

**Unlogged batches** skip the batch log and give no atomicity across partitions.

What batches are not: a way to load lots of data fast. A batch spanning many partitions makes one coordinator do all the work and hold everything in memory, instead of spreading the writes across the cluster. For many independent writes, send separate statements from your application at the same time (**in parallel**); drivers can send each one straight to a replica that owns it (see the drivers lesson).

Cassandra warns when a batch is larger than `batch_size_warn_threshold` (5 KiB, about 5,000 bytes, by default) and rejects it above `batch_size_fail_threshold` (50 KiB).

Counter updates can only be batched with other counter updates (`BEGIN COUNTER BATCH`).
takeaways: Logged batches guarantee all statements eventually apply
No isolation across partitions and no rollback
Single-partition batches are atomic, isolated and cheap
Don't use multi-partition batches for bulk loading
pitfalls: Batching thousands of unrelated rows to 'speed up' inserts, swamping a single coordinator.

quiz.q: What does a logged batch spanning two partitions guarantee?
options: Readers never see a partial result
It is faster than separate writes
All statements eventually apply, even if the coordinator fails
It rolls back on any error
quiz.explain: The batchlog ensures eventual atomicity, but not isolation or speed.

concepts.name: Drivers, prepared statements and paging
concepts.summary: Connect from application code with a driver, and use prepared statements, token-aware routing, asynchronous queries and automatic paging.
concepts.why: How fast an application runs on Cassandra depends as much on how it uses the driver as on the tables.
concepts.body:
Applications use a driver (for Java, Python, Go, Node.js, C#...) that speaks Cassandra's own **protocol**, its rules for messages, on port 9042. The core habits are the same in every language.

Create one `session` per application and reuse it. It keeps a set of open connections to every node, a **connection pool**, because opening a new connection for each request is slow.

Use prepared statements for anything you run repeatedly. Cassandra reads and checks the statement once; the values are sent separately, so nobody can sneak extra CQL in through them; and the driver learns which values form the partition key.

Keep the default **token-aware routing**: the driver computes the token of each request's partition key and sends the request straight to a replica, skipping a hop through another node. It's combined with a data-center-aware policy, so requests stay in your local data center.

Set the consistency level per statement, or once as a default (`LOCAL_QUORUM` is typical).

Send independent writes **asynchronously**: start many without waiting for each answer, then collect the results, with a cap on how many are outstanding at once. That beats putting them in a batch.

Large results come back a page at a time (**paging**): the driver fetches `fetch_size` rows (5000 by default) at a time as your loop moves through them. If your service keeps nothing in memory between requests (it's **stateless**), hand the driver's paging state to the client and resume from it on the next request.

Mark statements idempotent when they are (most upserts are; counter updates and list appends aren't). Then, after a **timeout** (no answer in time), the driver may safely retry, or even send an early second copy to another replica (speculative execution).

Don't send `null` for missing values; leave them unset to avoid tombstones.
concepts.code:
from datetime import date, datetime, timezone
from cassandra.cluster import Cluster, ExecutionProfile, EXEC_PROFILE_DEFAULT
from cassandra.policies import DCAwareRoundRobinPolicy, TokenAwarePolicy
from cassandra import ConsistencyLevel

profile = ExecutionProfile(
    load_balancing_policy=TokenAwarePolicy(DCAwareRoundRobinPolicy(local_dc="datacenter1")),
    consistency_level=ConsistencyLevel.LOCAL_QUORUM)
cluster = Cluster(["10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2"], execution_profiles={EXEC_PROFILE_DEFAULT: profile})
session = cluster.connect("shop")                 # one session per app

insert = session.prepare("INSERT INTO readings (sensor_id, day, ts, value) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)")
insert.is_idempotent = True
day = date(2026, 10, 17)
rows = [(day, datetime(2026, 10, 17, 9, m, tzinfo=timezone.utc), 20 + m / 10) for m in range(60)]
# start all writes at once, then wait for each result
futures = [session.execute_async(insert, ("s-17", day, ts, v)) for day, ts, v in rows]
for f in futures:
    f.result()                                    # raise on failure

select = session.prepare("SELECT ts, value FROM readings WHERE sensor_id = ? AND day = ?")
for row in session.execute(select, ("s-17", day)):  # pages transparently
    print(row.ts, row.value)
takeaways: One long-lived `session` per application
Prepared statements: checked once, safe values, enable token-aware routing
Run independent writes asynchronously in parallel, not in batches
Results page automatically; mark idempotent statements
pitfalls: Building CQL text by pasting values in (f-strings) for every request: the driver can't tell which replica to send it to, Cassandra re-reads every statement, and CQL injection becomes possible.

quiz.q: Why do prepared statements make token-aware routing possible?
options: They are cached on the client
The driver knows which bound values are the partition key, so it can compute the token
quiz.explain: Preparation returns metadata identifying partition key columns, letting the driver pick a replica.

concepts.name: Storage-attached indexes (SAI)
concepts.summary: Query non-key columns with SAI indexes in Cassandra 5.0, including ranges and vector similarity search, and know when an index is the wrong tool.
concepts.why: SAI makes extra ways of looking up data practical, but only if you understand how an index query runs across the cluster.
concepts.body:
Cassandra 5.0's **Storage-Attached Indexing** (SAI) indexes regular columns, clustering columns, collections and vectors. On every node, each index is built right next to the table's data (both the in-memory part holding new writes and each file on disk), so it's created, merged and deleted together with the data. That makes it much more efficient than the older secondary indexes.

Create one with `CREATE INDEX ON t (col) USING 'sai';`. Then you can filter on that column: equality, ranges on numbers and dates, `CONTAINS` on collections, and several indexed columns combined with `AND`. Text indexes can ignore upper and lower case with options like `'case_sensitive': false`.

How the query runs matters:

- **with** the partition key given, an SAI query reads one partition: fast and cheap,
- **without** it, the coordinator must ask nodes covering the whole token ring, so latency grows with the size of the cluster. That's fine for occasional or admin queries with **selective** conditions (that match few rows) and a `LIMIT`, not for your busiest request path.

For **vector search**, finding the stored vectors closest to a given one (with embeddings: the most similar in meaning), index a `vector<float, n>` column and query with `ORDER BY embedding ANN OF [ ... ] LIMIT k`, optionally combined with other SAI filters.

Indexes cost extra write work and disk space on every node. If a non-key query is central and very frequent, a dedicated denormalized table is still the most predictable design; SAI fills the gaps for additional, less frequent queries.
takeaways: SAI (5.0) indexes columns next to the data on each node
Combine indexed columns with AND, ranges and CONTAINS
Give the partition key when you can; otherwise the query asks every node
Vector search: ORDER BY col ANN OF [...] LIMIT k
pitfalls: Putting a cluster-wide SAI query, without a partition key, on the busiest request path.

quiz.q: Why can an SAI query without a partition key get slower as the cluster grows?
options: The coordinator must query nodes covering the whole token range
SAI indexes are stored on one node
quiz.explain: Each node indexes only its own data, so a query without a partition key has to ask across the ring.

concepts.name: Lightweight transactions (compare-and-set)
concepts.summary: Use IF NOT EXISTS and IF conditions for check-then-write operations on a single partition that all replicas agree on, and know their cost.
concepts.why: Uniqueness and check-then-act operations (usernames, inventory) need more than last-write-wins.
concepts.body:
Plain writes overwrite blindly. When you need to check something before writing, Cassandra offers **lightweight transactions** (LWT): conditional writes in which the replicas first agree on the outcome using **Paxos**, a voting procedure that lets several machines settle on exactly one result. That makes them **linearizable** for that partition: everyone sees the operations happen one at a time in a single order, as if there were only one copy.

- `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS` claims a key only if it's free, e.g. a unique username,
- `UPDATE ... SET qty = 4 WHERE ... IF qty = 5` changes a value only if it still has the expected one,
- `DELETE ... IF EXISTS` and `UPDATE ... IF EXISTS` act only on rows that exist.

The result contains an `[applied]` column; when it's false, the result also shows the current values so you can decide what to do.

The Paxos vote uses the **serial consistency level**: `SERIAL` (across data centers) or `LOCAL_SERIAL`; the write itself uses the normal consistency level. Read with `SERIAL` if you must see the result of lightweight transactions still in progress.

Costs and limits:

- several round trips, so roughly 4 times the latency of a normal write, and many clients competing for the same partition cause timeouts,
- conditions are limited to one partition; there are no multi-partition transactions yet (general ACID transactions via the Accord protocol are planned for a later major version),
- mixing LWT and plain writes on the same data breaks the guarantees.

Use LWTs for the rare operations that truly need them, not for every write.
concepts.code:
-- unique username claim
INSERT INTO shop.usernames (username, user_id)
VALUES ('ana', 5b6962dd-3f90-4c93-8f61-eabfa4a803e2) IF NOT EXISTS;
--  [applied]
--       True
INSERT INTO shop.usernames (username, user_id)
VALUES ('ana', 0d1d8cd6-31ab-4a4b-a6d3-6c0e2b1b9a10) IF NOT EXISTS;
--  [applied] | username | user_id
--      False |      ana | 5b6962dd-3f90-4c93-8f61-eabfa4a803e2

-- optimistic stock decrement
SERIAL CONSISTENCY LOCAL_SERIAL;
UPDATE shop.stock SET qty = 4 WHERE sku = 'PEN' IF qty = 5;
--  [applied] | qty
--      False |   3      -> re-read and retry with the current value
takeaways: IF NOT EXISTS / IF col = value give compare-and-set via Paxos
Check the [applied] column; failures return current values
Serial CL governs the Paxos phase (SERIAL or LOCAL_SERIAL)
Single-partition only and several times slower than plain writes
pitfalls: Mixing conditional and unconditional writes to the same column, which can silently break linearizability.

quiz.q: Two users try to register the username "ana" at the same time with INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS. What happens?
options: Both succeed and the last write wins
quiz.explain: Paxos serializes the conditional inserts so only one applies.

concepts.name: Partition sizing, bucketing and hot spots
concepts.summary: Keep partitions bounded with time or hash buckets, and estimate partition size before a table goes live.
concepts.why: Unbounded and hot partitions are the most common cause of Cassandra performance incidents.
concepts.body:
A partition lives on RF nodes and is read as a unit, so both its size and its traffic matter:

- **too big**: very large partitions (rule of thumb: keep them under about 100 MB and 100,000 rows, ideally much smaller) slow down reads, compaction, repair and the copying of data between nodes (**streaming**),
- **too hot**: one partition key getting a big share of the traffic (a celebrity user, a global counter) swamps its replicas while the rest of the cluster sits idle. That's a **hot partition**.

**Bucketing** adds a part to the partition key to limit how much one partition collects:

- **time buckets**: `((sensor_id, day), ts)` instead of `((sensor_id), ts)`; pick the bucket size (hour, day, month) so one bucket holds a manageable amount even at the busiest rate,
- **hash buckets**: `((channel_id, bucket), ts)` with `bucket = hash(msg_id) % 8` spreads a hot key over 8 partitions; readers query all 8 and merge the results.

Bucketing costs reads: a query covering a week of daily buckets needs 7 queries (send them at the same time).

Estimate before launch: rows per partition = rate x bucket duration; size = rows x (bytes per row + extra bookkeeping per row). Then check with `nodetool tablehistograms`, which shows partition size **percentiles** (for example the size 99% of partitions stay under), and `nodetool tablestats` (the largest partition). Cassandra 5.0 can also warn or refuse when partitions get too big, using **guardrails** such as `partition_size_warn_threshold`.
concepts.code:
-- Unbounded: one partition per sensor grows forever
--   PRIMARY KEY ((sensor_id), ts)

-- Bounded: one partition per sensor per day
CREATE TABLE shop.readings_by_day (
  sensor_id text, day date, ts timestamp, value double,
  PRIMARY KEY ((sensor_id, day), ts)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC);

-- Estimate: 1 reading/s -> 86,400 rows/day x ~40 bytes = ~3.5 MB per partition: OK

-- A week of data = 7 partition reads, issued concurrently by the app
SELECT ts, value FROM shop.readings_by_day WHERE sensor_id = 's-17' AND day = '2026-10-17';

-- $ nodetool tablehistograms shop readings_by_day
--   Percentile  Partition Size  Cell Count ...
--   99%         3.97 MiB        86400
takeaways: Keep partitions bounded (well under ~100 MB) and traffic evenly spread
Time buckets limit growth; hash buckets split hot keys
Estimate rows and bytes per partition before launch
Check nodetool tablehistograms and tablestats on the live cluster
pitfalls: Partitioning event data only by user or device id, creating partitions that grow forever.

quiz.q: A sensor writes 100 readings per second. Which partition key keeps partitions reasonably small?
quiz.explain: At 360,000 rows per hour bucket the partition stays bounded; per-year or per-sensor would grow huge.

concepts.name: Storage engine: commit log, memtables, SSTables
concepts.summary: Follow writes through the commit log and memtable to immutable SSTables, and reads through bloom filters, indexes and compaction.
concepts.why: Write speed, read latency and disk usage all follow from how Cassandra's storage engine lays data out on disk.
concepts.body:
The **storage engine** is the part of a database that decides how data is laid out on disk and read back. Cassandra's is a **log-structured merge tree** (LSM tree): new writes collect in memory, are written out as sorted files, and the files are merged in the background.

**Write path** on each replica: the write is appended to the commit log (for safety; by default `commitlog_sync` is `periodic`, forcing the log onto disk every 10 seconds) and added to a **memtable**, a sorted table kept in memory, one per table. Nothing on disk is read or changed, which is why writes are fast. When a memtable fills up, it's **flushed** to disk as a new SSTable, which is never changed afterwards, and the matching part of the commit log can be reused.

**Read path**: a partition's data may be spread over the memtable and several SSTables, so a read merges them, keeping the newest cell by timestamp and applying tombstones. To avoid opening every SSTable, each has a **Bloom filter** (a tiny structure that answers "this partition is definitely not in this file" or "maybe"), a partition index and summaries held in memory. Cassandra 5.0 adds the BTI SSTable format and memtables built on tries (compact trees of shared key prefixes), which use less memory. Row and key caches are optional extras.

**Compaction** merges SSTables in the background, keeping the newest version of each cell and dropping tombstones older than `gc_grace_seconds`. The strategy is set per table:

- `SizeTieredCompactionStrategy`: best for heavy writing; needs spare disk space for merges,
- `LeveledCompactionStrategy`: best for heavy reading; more disk reads and writes,
- `TimeWindowCompactionStrategy`: for time series with a TTL,
- `UnifiedCompactionStrategy` (5.0): can be set up to behave like either of the first two.

How many SSTables a read touches (see `nodetool tablehistograms`) is a key health **metric**.
concepts.code:
-- per-table compaction choice
ALTER TABLE shop.readings_by_day
  WITH compaction = {'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy',
                     'compaction_window_unit': 'DAYS', 'compaction_window_size': 1};

ALTER TABLE shop.users
  WITH compaction = {'class': 'UnifiedCompactionStrategy'};   -- 5.0

-- $ nodetool flush shop users            # memtable -> new SSTable
-- $ nodetool tablestats shop.users       # SSTable count, bloom filter false ratio
-- $ nodetool tablehistograms shop users  # SSTables touched per read (percentiles)
-- $ nodetool compactionstats             # running and pending compactions
takeaways: Writes: commit log + memtable, flushed to immutable SSTables
Reads merge memtable and SSTables, newest timestamp wins
Bloom filters and indexes skip SSTables that can't contain the partition
Compaction merges SSTables; strategy is chosen per table
pitfalls: Picking LeveledCompactionStrategy for a write-heavy time-series table and drowning in compaction disk work.

quiz.q: Why are Cassandra writes cheap compared with in-place update databases?
options: They only append to the commit log and update an in-memory memtable, with no read before write
They are buffered on the client
They write to one replica only
quiz.explain: The log-structured design never reads or rewrites existing data on the write path.

concepts.name: Tombstones, gc_grace and repair
concepts.summary: Understand how tombstones affect reads, why repair must run within gc_grace_seconds, and how to avoid resurrected data.
concepts.why: Slow, tombstone-heavy reads and deleted data coming back are classic Cassandra failures on live clusters, and both are preventable.
concepts.body:
Deletes, TTL expiry and null writes leave tombstones. They must be kept for a while. Suppose a replica was down during a delete, and the tombstone were removed everywhere else before that replica heard about it: its old value would then look like the only copy and come back at the next sync. This is **zombie data** (also called resurrected data).

So tombstones are kept for **gc_grace_seconds** (default 864000, 10 days), and the rule is: **every replica must be repaired within gc_grace_seconds**. Repair compares replicas using **Merkle trees** (trees of hashes that quickly show which ranges of data differ) and streams over only the differences. Run it routinely, e.g. `nodetool repair -pr` on each node in turn, or through an automated tool, and prefer incremental repair, which only handles data not yet repaired. Hints and read repair help, but don't replace it.

Tombstones also slow down **reads**: a query over a range must read every tombstone in it to know what's deleted. Cassandra writes a warning to its log after `tombstone_warn_threshold` (1000) tombstones in one query, and aborts the query at `tombstone_failure_threshold` (100,000).

Avoiding tombstone trouble:

- don't use a table as a queue (insert rows, delete them when done, and always read from the start),
- don't write nulls; leave columns unset,
- prefer replacing frozen collections to overwriting large non-frozen ones (overwriting a non-frozen collection writes a tombstone covering the old contents),
- for time series, use a TTL with TWCS and query only recent time windows,
- lower `gc_grace_seconds` only if repairs reliably run more often than that.
concepts.code:
-- anti-pattern: a queue table; readers scan past ever more tombstones
CREATE TABLE shop.jobs (queue text, id timeuuid, payload text, PRIMARY KEY (queue, id));
DELETE FROM shop.jobs WHERE queue = 'email' AND id = 50554d6e-29bb-11ef-9f3c-0242ac120002;
SELECT * FROM shop.jobs WHERE queue = 'email' LIMIT 1;   -- reads every tombstone first
-- WARN ... Read 1 live rows and 25000 tombstone cells for query ...

ALTER TABLE shop.jobs WITH gc_grace_seconds = 864000;   -- 10 days (the default)

-- $ nodetool repair -pr shop          # primary ranges of this node, run on every node
-- $ nodetool repair --full shop       # full rather than incremental
-- $ nodetool tablestats shop.jobs     # "Average tombstones per slice"
takeaways: Tombstones live for gc_grace_seconds (10 days default)
Repair every replica within gc_grace or deleted data can come back
Reads must scan tombstones; queries warn at 1000 and fail at 100,000
Avoid queue-like tables, null writes and needless collection overwrites
pitfalls: Lowering gc_grace_seconds to shrink tombstones without making repairs run more often, resurrecting deleted data.

quiz.q: A node was down for two weeks, longer than gc_grace_seconds, while rows were deleted. What is the risk when it rejoins?
options: The node's data is automatically wiped
Deleted rows can reappear because the tombstones were already purged elsewhere
quiz.explain: Its stale copies have no tombstone left to shadow them; the node should be rebuilt or replaced instead.

concepts.name: Token ring, vnodes, gossip and snitches
concepts.summary: Understand how nodes own token ranges via vnodes, discover each other through gossip, and place replicas with snitches.
concepts.why: Scaling, replacing nodes and multi-DC topologies all depend on how the ring is laid out and how nodes coordinate.
concepts.body:
**Partitioner and tokens.** The **partitioner**, normally `Murmur3Partitioner`, hashes each partition key to a 64-bit token. All possible tokens form the **token ring**, and each node owns ranges of it. A partition's first replica is the node owning its token; further replicas are found by walking on around the ring.

**Virtual nodes.** Rather than one big range, each node owns many small ones, called **vnodes** (`num_tokens`, 16 by default since 4.0, placed by an algorithm that keeps ownership balanced). Adding or removing a node then moves small slices from many other nodes, spreading the streaming work.

**Replica placement.** `NetworkTopologyStrategy` places replicas per data center and, using the **snitch**, on different **racks** (cabinets of servers sharing power and network) where possible, so one rack failing doesn't take out every copy. `GossipingPropertyFileSnitch`, where each node declares its data center and rack in `cassandra-rackdc.properties`, is the standard choice.

**Gossip.** Every second, each node swaps state (up or down, load, schema version, tokens) with a few other nodes, so news about the cluster spreads to everyone like a rumour, with no master. The **phi accrual failure detector** turns how late a node's gossip messages are into a level of suspicion, and marks the node down when it gets too high.

**Coordinators** send requests to replicas, keep hints for replicas that are down, and use the dynamic snitch's scores to prefer fast replicas for reads.

Operations follow from this: `nodetool status` shows each node's state, load and ownership; a new node joining (bootstrapping) streams in its ranges; `nodetool decommission` streams them away; and `nodetool cleanup` removes data a node no longer owns after others have joined.
concepts.code:
# $ nodetool status shop
# Datacenter: dc1
# Status=Up/Down  State=Normal/Leaving/Joining/Moving
# --  Address   Load      Tokens  Owns (effective)  Host ID   Rack
# UN  10.0.0.1  412 GiB   16      75.0%             8d5e...   r1
# UN  10.0.0.2  398 GiB   16      75.0%             1f2a...   r2
# UN  10.0.0.3  405 GiB   16      75.0%             c3b7...   r3
# DN  10.0.0.4  401 GiB   16      75.0%             9e04...   r1

# cassandra.yaml
#   num_tokens: 16
#   endpoint_snitch: GossipingPropertyFileSnitch
# cassandra-rackdc.properties
#   dc=dc1
#   rack=r1

# $ nodetool getendpoints shop users 5b6962dd-3f90-4c93-8f61-eabfa4a803e2
# $ nodetool cleanup shop     # after adding nodes, drop ranges no longer owned
takeaways: Murmur3 tokens map partitions onto a ring of node-owned ranges
vnodes (num_tokens 16) spread ownership and streaming load
Snitch + NetworkTopologyStrategy place replicas across racks and DCs
Gossip and the phi accrual detector manage membership without a master
pitfalls: Forgetting nodetool cleanup after adding nodes, so old nodes keep data they no longer own.

quiz.q: How does a Cassandra node learn that another node joined or went down?
options: Through gossip exchanged with peers every second
quiz.explain: Gossip spreads state peer to peer, and the failure detector marks unresponsive nodes down.
